title: Do Not Forsake Me, O LORD
superscription: A Psalm of David, for remembrance.

verses.text: O LORD, do not rebuke me in Your anger or discipline me in Your wrath.
For Your arrows have pierced me deeply, and Your hand has pressed down on me.
There is no soundness in my body because of Your anger; there is no rest in my bones because of my sin.
For my iniquities have overwhelmed me; they are a burden too heavy to bear.
My wounds are foul and festering because of my sinful folly.
I am bent and brought low; all day long I go about mourning.
For my loins are full of burning pain, and no soundness remains in my body.
I am numb and badly crushed; I groan in anguish of heart.
O Lord, my every desire is before You; my groaning is not hidden from You.
My heart pounds, my strength fails, and even the light of my eyes has faded.
My beloved and friends shun my disease, and my kinsmen stand at a distance.
Those who seek my life lay snares; those who wish me harm speak destruction, plotting deceit all day long.
But like a deaf man, I do not hear; and like a mute man, I do not open my mouth.
I am like a man who cannot hear, whose mouth offers no reply.
I wait for You, O LORD; You will answer, O Lord my God.
For I said, "Let them not gloat over me— those who taunt me when my foot slips."
For I am ready to fall, and my pain is ever with me.
Yes, I confess my iniquity; I am troubled by my sin.
Many are my enemies without cause, and many hate me without reason.
Those who repay my good with evil attack me for pursuing the good.
Do not forsake me, O LORD; be not far from me, O my God.
Come quickly to help me, O Lord my Savior.

context.author: The title says “of David” (Hebrew le-David), which can mean by David, for David or about David. Seventy-three psalms carry his name; tradition and the New Testament take many of them as his.
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship in Jerusalem, and every reader who prays
context.setting: The title says it is “for remembrance.” Like Psalm 6, it begins, “O LORD, do not rebuke me in Your anger” (v.1). David is sick and knows why: “there is no rest in my bones because of my sin. For my iniquities have overwhelmed me; they are a burden too heavy to bear” (vv.3-4). His wounds fester, he is bent over and burning with pain (vv.5-8). “O Lord, my every desire is before You” (v.9). Friends stand at a distance (v.11), enemies plot, and he keeps silent “like a deaf man” (v.13), waiting for God to answer (v.15). “Yes, I confess my iniquity” (v.18). He ends, “Do not forsake me, O LORD… Come quickly to help me, O Lord my Savior” (vv.21-22).
context.custom: Skin diseases and festering sores could make a person unclean and force them to live apart (Leviticus 13:45-46), which may be why friends kept away. “For remembrance” may connect the psalm with the memorial portion of the grain offering (Leviticus 2:2), or simply mean a prayer asking God to remember.
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 39 reflects on how fleeting life is: “each man at his best exists as but a breath.”
context.timelineBible: At the crucifixion Jesus’ acquaintances “stood at a distance” (Luke 23:49), as David’s friends do in v.11. Jesus, like the sufferer of v.13, was silent before His accusers: “He did not open His mouth” (Isaiah 53:7; Matthew 27:12-14). This is one of the seven penitential psalms.

translation.meaning: Sin, missing the mark; also the sin offering.
Stroke, plague, affliction, a skin disease.

gospelParallels.note: His acquaintances stood at a distance.
He gave no answer, not even to a single charge.
The Lord disciplines the one He loves.

otBackground.note: Do not rebuke me in Your anger.
He must live alone, outside the camp.
He did not open His mouth.

overview.summary: Sick, in pain and abandoned by friends because of his sin, David confesses his iniquity, waits silently for God, and asks the LORD not to forsake him.
overview.settingLine: A sickbed, with friends keeping their distance.

archaeology.t: Clay models of body parts were offered at Asclepius shrines in the Greek world.
Babylonian tablets list symptoms and treatments.

overview.discussion: David names both his sin and his suffering, and brings both to God (vv.4, 9). Do I hide either from Him?
overview.book: The book of Psalms · 150 psalms (1-20 in the app so far). Israel’s songs and prayers: praise, lament, thanks, trust and wisdom, many of them by David.
overview.author: David
